Acute chest syndrome: Young children present with chest pain, fever, cough, tachypnea, leukocytosis, and pulmonary infiltrates in the upper lobes; adults are usually afebrile, dyspneic with severe chest pain, with multilobar/lower lobe disease

Acute chest syndrome refers to a life-threatening pulmonary complication of sickle cell disease defined as a new radiodensity on chest radiography plus any 2 of the following: fever, respiratory distress, hypoxia, cough, and chest pain.
Acute chest syndrome needs a cephalosporin plus a macrolide to cover typical and atypical organisms.

snip.t: Sickle Cell Disease: Can present with acute chest syndrome, which may involve pericardial inflammation or effusion.
Obstructive: Extracardiac flow obstruction — Pericardial tamponade (TB pericarditis), tension pneumothorax, pulmonary embolism, sickle cell acute chest syndrome
Sickle Cell Disease: Precipitates hypovolemic shock (splenic sequestration crisis in children) or obstructive shock (acute chest syndrome with cor pulmonale).
Chest findings (crepitations, tachypnoea): Acute chest syndrome – pulmonary vaso‑occlusion, infection, or fat embolism.

qs.q: A young patient with sickle cell disease develops fever, cough, tachypnea, chest pain, and hypoxia following a painful episode. What is a key mechanism or origin of this life-threatening acute chest syndrome?
o: Primary bacterial colonization of the pleural cavity by bacteria
Direct infiltration of the lung parenchyma by malignant cells
Fat embolism originating from the distal bone during a crisis
Massive autoimmune destruction of circulating platelets in vessels
qs.e: Acute chest syndrome can be triggered by hypoventilation during a vaso-occlusive crisis or as a result of fat embolism originating from the distal bone. It accounts for 25% of deaths in these patients.

qs.q: In addition to supplemental oxygen, which intervention is essential when managing acute chest syndrome?
qs.e: Empiric antibiotics cover possible bacterial pneumonia contributing to ACS. The other measures are not standard initial therapy.

faq.a: The cephalosporin covers typical bacteria (e.g., S. pneumoniae) while the macrolide treats atypical organisms (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia) that are common triggers of ACS.
faq.q: Why give both a cephalosporin and a macrolide?

faq.a: Yes, severe malaria can precipitate pulmonary sequestration and vaso‑occlusion, so a positive rapid test warrants antimalarial therapy alongside standard ACS treatment.
When haemoglobin falls > 2 g/dL from baseline, or when hypoxia persists despite O₂, indicating severe sickling‑related anemia.

exam: A 7‑year‑old with sickle cell disease presents with fever, cough and new right‑upper‑lobe infiltrate. What is the next immediate step? — Start empiric ceftriaxone plus azithromycin and give supplemental O₂ to keep SpO₂ ≥ 92 %.
How does ACS differ from a simple vaso‑occlusive pain crisis? — ACS has a new pulmonary infiltrate and respiratory compromise; pain crisis lacks infiltrate and hypoxia.
A patient on hydroxyurea develops ACS but cannot receive a chest X‑ray. What alternative investigation can you use? — Perform bedside lung ultrasound to look for consolidations or effusion.

Why is a macrolide preferred over a fluoroquinolone in this setting? — Macrolides cover atypical pathogens common in children and have a safer profile in sickle cell patients; fluoroquinolones have higher risk of tendon toxicity and are not first‑line for community pneumonia.
What red‑flag sign would prompt transfer to a higher‑level facility? — SpO₂ < 85 % despite high‑flow O₂ or development of hypotension (SBP < 90 mmHg).
Explain the role of hydroxyurea in preventing future episodes of ACS. — Hydroxyurea increases fetal haemoglobin, reducing sickling and vaso‑occlusion, thereby lowering ACS incidence.

A patient with ACS also tests positive for malaria. How does this affect management? — Add parenteral artesunate (or appropriate antimalarial) to the antibiotic regimen and monitor for worsening anemia.

What distinguishes ACS from pulmonary embolism on imaging? — ACS shows new infiltrates; pulmonary embolism often has normal X‑ray or wedge‑shaped infarct, and CT pulmonary angiography (if available) confirms embolus.
ai.title: Acute Chest Syndrome
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Acute chest syndrome (ACS) is a life‑threatening pulmonary complication of sickle cell disease, defined by new infiltrate plus fever, cough, chest pain or hypoxia. Prompt recognition, supportive care and targeted antibiotics are essential, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: ACS is diagnosed when a patient with sickle cell disease develops a new radiographic pulmonary infiltrate together with any one of: fever, chest pain, cough, tachypnoea, dyspnoea, or hypoxia (SpO₂ < 92%). The infiltrate must not be explained by heart failure alone.

t.b: Confirms new infiltrate and helps exclude pneumothorax or effusion; if unavailable, bedside lung ultrasound can detect consolidations.
Detects hypoxia; SpO₂ < 92 % indicates need for supplemental O₂.
Leukocytosis supports infection; a drop in haemoglobin may suggest concurrent vaso‑occlusive crisis.

b: Moderate: O₂ ≥ 2 L/min to keep SpO₂ ≥ 92 %
Severe: O₂ ≥ 5 L/min, rising lactate, hypotension, or organ failure
sections.p: Severity is graded by respiratory compromise and organ dysfunction. Mild disease has SpO₂ ≥ 92 % on room air; moderate requires O₂ ≥ 2 L/min; severe needs ≥ 5 L/min or non‑invasive ventilation, or shows rising lactate, hypotension, or multi‑organ failure.

b: Typical bacterial pneumonia (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae)
sections.p: ACS results from pulmonary vaso‑occlusion, infection, or fat embolism. In East Africa, bacterial pneumonia (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae) and atypical organisms (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia) are common, as are malaria‑related sequestration and TB pleuritis.

Children often have fever, cough, chest pain and upper‑lobe infiltrates; adults may be afebrile, present with severe dyspnoea, chest pain and multilobar or lower‑lobe infiltrates. Tachypnoea, use of accessory muscles and hypoxia are key bedside clues.
Prioritise bedside tools; send blood for cultures if possible, but start empiric antibiotics without delay.

t.b: Identify bloodstream pathogen; if unavailable, treat empirically for typical and atypical bacteria.
Detects malaria which can precipitate ACS; a positive test adds antimalarial therapy.
Detects consolidations, pleural effusion, or pneumothorax; guides need for drainage.

sections.p: Rapidly falling SpO₂, rising lactate, hypotension, or new cardiac murmur suggest impending shock, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) or cor pulmonale.

b: Empiric ceftriaxone + azithromycin (or erythromycin) – covers S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, Mycoplasma, Chlamydia
Add artesunate if rapid malaria test positive
O₂ supplementation to keep SpO₂ ≥ 92 %; consider CPAP if severe
Analgesia and incentive spirometry to prevent atelectasis
Transfusion if Hb falls >2 g/dL or severe hypoxia
sections.p: Treat infection first, then provide supportive care and monitor for deterioration. Use a third‑generation cephalosporin plus a macrolide to cover typical and atypical organisms; add antimalarial or anti‑TB therapy if indicated.

b: Start or optimise hydroxyurea to reduce sickling
Educate patient/family on early signs of ACS
sections.p: After discharge, ensure vaccination (pneumococcal, Hib, influenza), hydroxyurea optimisation, and education on early reporting of chest symptoms.

b: Vaso‑occlusive crisis – no new infiltrate, no hypoxia
Simple pneumonia – no sickle‑cell‑related vaso‑occlusion, may lack chest pain
Pulmonary embolism – sudden dyspnoea, often normal chest X‑ray, risk factors differ
sections.p: Distinguish ACS from simple vaso‑occlusive pain crisis, pneumonia unrelated to sickle cell, pulmonary embolism, and TB pleuritis.

b: Normal WBC does not rule out infection in sickle cell
Early X‑ray may be normal; repeat after 24 h if clinical suspicion remains
sections.p: Leukocytosis may be absent if the patient is immunocompromised; a normal chest X‑ray early in disease does not exclude ACS – repeat imaging if symptoms persist.
